p: I come now to my own present, and to things which I can see from my window, or nearly. It is a strange sensation for a historian. All my life I have looked backward. Here I must look about me, and also, by means of the pages from the future, a little way ahead, and report what my neighbours do not yet know: that several of the curious machines being tinkered with in the workshops of our day will, within a generation, change the daily life of every household in the civilised world.
## The telegraph, and the voice along the wire

Electricity is not new to us. The electric telegraph has been in use since the eighteen-forties; Mr Wheatstone and Mr Cooke in England, and Mr Morse in America, devised methods of sending messages along a wire by pulses of current, and today there are telegraph wires along every railway and cables beneath the Atlantic, laid, after many failures, by the Great Eastern steamship in eighteen sixty-six. A message from London reaches New York in minutes. That alone would make our age remarkable. But the telegraph speaks only in a code of clicks, which must be translated by a trained clerk. It cannot carry the human voice.

Many men are at this moment trying to make it do so. The Encyclopaedia tells me that the one who will succeed, or at any rate who will receive the patent, is a young Scotsman living in Boston, Alexander Graham Bell, a teacher of the deaf, whose father invented a system of symbols for teaching speech. On the seventh of March next year, eighteen seventy-six, he will be granted an American patent for an apparatus for transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically, and three days later, by the account in his notebook, he will speak into his instrument the words: Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you. And his assistant Thomas Watson, in another room, will hear him.

I must add, as the Encyclopaedia scrupulously does, that the priority of the invention will be bitterly disputed. On the very same day that Bell's lawyer filed his application, an American named Elisha Gray filed a notice of a similar invention, and there will be accusations of improper dealing at the Patent Office that are argued over to this day. An Italian in New York, Antonio Meucci, had made a speaking apparatus years before, but was too poor to keep up his provisional patent. And in Germany a schoolmaster, Johann Philipp Reis, has already made an instrument he calls the telephone, from Greek words meaning far sound, which carries musical tones and, some say, speech. Great inventions, I have observed, are rarely the work of one man; they are in the air, and several men reach for them at once, and the lawyers decide which of them caught it.

Within a few years, the Encyclopaedia tells me, there will be telephone exchanges in every great city, staffed by young women who connect the calls by hand; within fifty years, telephones in most middle-class houses; and within a century and a half, a telephone without any wire at all, in the pocket of nearly every person on earth, which also serves as a library, a newspaper, a map and a gramophone. Mrs Pruett, when I described this to her, said that it sounded like a great nuisance, and I am not sure she is wrong.
## The engine that burns its fuel within

The steam engine burns its fuel outside itself, under a boiler, and must carry a great weight of water and iron. For many years inventors have tried to make an engine in which the fuel burns inside the cylinder itself, so that the explosion of a mixture of gas and air drives the piston directly. A Belgian, Étienne Lenoir, built such an engine in Paris some fifteen years ago, burning coal gas, and it runs, after a fashion, though it drinks gas at a ruinous rate. In Germany, at a works near Cologne, Mr Nikolaus Otto and his partner Eugen Langen make engines of this kind for small workshops. The pages from the future inform me that next year, in eighteen seventy-six, Otto will build an engine working on four strokes, drawing in the mixture, compressing it, firing it and expelling the smoke, which will become the pattern of almost every such engine thereafter.

Then Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, who work for Otto, will make the engine small and fast, running on a light spirit distilled from petroleum, which our lamps already burn as paraffin; and in eighteen eighty-five and six, Karl Benz of Mannheim will build a carriage that moves by its own engine, without a horse. His wife Bertha, I am delighted to learn, will take it without telling him on a journey of some sixty miles to visit her mother, stopping at an apothecary's shop to buy fuel, and so prove to the world that it is practical. In the following century these motor-cars will multiply beyond counting, and the streets of every city will be given over to them. Rudolf Diesel will make an engine that fires its fuel by compression alone. And, in nineteen hundred and three, two bicycle makers of Ohio named Wright will fit a petrol engine to a flying machine of their own design and fly, for twelve seconds, over the sands of North Carolina. Within seventy years men will fly in machines of a different kind to the moon.

I am told that the vast quantities of petroleum consumed by these engines will make the countries that possess it rich and much fought over, and that the smoke of them, together with that of coal, will warm the very climate of the earth. The men of the future are trying, in consequence, to return to engines driven by electricity, which is a curious end to the story.

Of electricity itself, the great discoveries are already made. Mr Faraday, at the Royal Institution, showed in eighteen thirty-one that moving a magnet near a coil of wire produces a current, which is the principle of every electric generator, and Professor Clerk Maxwell, now at Cambridge, has shown in mathematics that light itself is a wave of electricity and magnetism. Arc lamps, which make a blinding light by a spark between rods of carbon, light a few lighthouses and public places. What is wanted is a small, steady light for a house.

The Encyclopaedia tells me that, in eighteen seventy-nine, Mr Joseph Swan of Newcastle in England and Mr Thomas Edison of New Jersey in America will each make a practical electric lamp, a glass bulb emptied of air with a fine glowing thread inside it; and that they will, after some quarrelling, join their companies in England. Edison will open in eighteen eighty-two, in New York, the first central station supplying electric current to a district of the city. Then will follow a war of the currents, between Edison's system and that of George Westinghouse and a Serbian genius named Nikola Tesla, whose alternating current can be sent over long distances; and Tesla will win. Over the next half-century, electric power will be carried by wires to factories, trams, streets and at last to almost every house in the richer countries, and the night, which has divided the life of mankind since the beginning, will be abolished by the turning of a switch.

When I think of that, I think of the first hearth, a million years ago, and of the hours of light that fire added to the evening. Electricity has completed what fire began. I am not sure that we are the better for having no darkness left. But I should like, I confess, to read by an electric lamp before I die. My eyes are not what they were, and the gas makes Tacitus sneeze.
